Electronic EAPs offer a much more robust and practical alternative. Powered by electric fields that attract compliant electrodes (usually conductive carbon grease) stenciled onto each side of a flat polymer, these assemblies expand as the electrodes squeeze in and cause significant Maxwell stresses. Until now, Maxwell stress has generally been regarded as a side effect in polymers, generally not strong enough to offer practical actuation.⁴ However, the identification of soft polymer thin films with high dielectric breakdown strengths has led to exceptionally high performance in dielectric elastomers. Dielectric elastomers are simply the polymer with compliant electrodes stenciled on each side. The only draw back to this method is the high voltages needed (over 1 kV).

The operation of electronic EAPs is based on the aforementioned dielectric polymer “sandwich” where high voltage squeezes down on the polymer to create an expansion in area. Such elastomers have coupled squeezing and stretching stresses that are consolidated into an effective compressive stress, p, given by Equation1:⁵
p = ε εₒ E² = ε εₒ (V/z)² (Eqn. 1)

In this equation, εₒ is the permittivity of free space (8.85 X 10⁻¹² F/m), ε is the relative dielectric constant (Capacitance of our selected polymer/ Capacitance of Air). E represents the applied electric field, V is the applied voltage, and z is the thickness of our polymer film. The importance of super high voltages becomes evident when viewing this equation, as the pressure of squeeze is directly related to the square of the voltage. Thus, the most effective way to increase the pressure and thereby the actuation strength is to increase the voltage applied. This equation also reveals the importance of a high relative dielectric constant. This constant basically describes a specific material's resistance to electric flow. In this case, the constant refers to current flow through the polymer between the oppositely charged electrodes. Since the squeezing effect is achieved by trapping electrons in the electrodes and harnessing their attraction to the other side's opposite charge, any

flow or “leakage” through the polymer would effectively reduce the strain and subsequent strength of actuation. Thusly, any material that has a high ε while still delivering flexibility, relatively low density, and the other advantages associated with polymers will be a winner.

Through a trial and error process of material selection, researchers at SRI International have discovered that a cheap and common acrylic polymer manufactured by 3M that can deliver the needed compressive stresses for effective actuation. This polymer has been identified as VHB 4910. A further enticing study is one done by SRI researchers that determined that pre-straining the material actually increases performance by increasing the compressive stress. What is actually happening in this process is an increase in ε through the pre-strain. This phenomenon is not currently explained, but some SRI personnel have proposed an intriguing mechanism. They believe the stretching of VHB 4910 orients the molecular polymer chains along the axis of stretch, and this orderly arrangement seems to close molecular holes through which electrons could have previously penetrate.³ Thus the material's resistance to current increases.

In embarking upon the creation of an EAP actuator for LIMS, it is known that the following will be needed: A High Voltage source, conductive carbon grease for electrodes, VHB 4910, and an apparatus that can pre-strain the material yet still provide free range of motion in the direction normal to this pre-strain.

The entire device can be divided into two main components. One aspect of the device regulates and delivers High Voltage in a controlled manner. The other part fulfills the mechanical requirements of pre-strain while allowing free movement.

Literature calls for 980V when dealing with acrylic polymers.⁶ While LIMS does have variable 0-12 volt DC power supplies as well as variacs that are good up to 120V AC, such a high voltage would essentially require its own apparatus to be successfully delivered. This seemed daunting at first due to some confusion over budget limitations. While the NASA Jet Propulsion Laboratory's website on EAPs did point directly to EMCO's patented Voltage source as a convenient solution, this first-time researcher thought that the roughly $100 price tag deemed the device a non-possibility.
